headline: Outgoing After Midnight: Bass in the Inlet Hole, Weakfish Under the Bridge Lights
subhead: With the ocean roughed up and warm, the smart money's inside — working the dark water on the back half of the ebb.
body_markdown:
I made the call again this week to skip the dawn patrol and let the inlet come to me after dark. That's not stubbornness — it's math. The ocean side has been running better than 2 feet of leftover swell out of the southeast, water pushing 73 degrees off the Bight, and that kind of junk on the beach just isn't worth fighting when the real bite is fifty yards inside the jetty on the back half of an outgoing tide. So that's where I've been, rod tip low, eyes on the white water sliding off the north jetty rocks around midnight to 2 a.m.

The bass are there, but I want to be straight with you — it's not a blitz. It's a working bite. Two, maybe three keepers a trip in that deep hole on the ocean side of the inlet, mixed with a handful of shorts that keep you honest. The fish are stacking on the current seam where the outgoing water dumps out past the rocks and meets the flatter bay water — that seam is holding bait and holding fish. I've been soaking chunk bunker on a fish-finder rig, 3 ounces of lead to hold bottom against that push, and I've had my best luck in the last two hours of the ebb, right before the tide goes dead slack. If you're a plug guy, a black Danny swimming plug worked slow along that same seam has drawn a few solid strikes, but the bait guys are outfishing the lure guys right now — the fish are eating with their nose more than their eyes in this dirty, current-stirred water.

Bluefish are the other story at the inlet, and this part I don't have to sell you on. There's a real wave of big blues moving through the East End right now, and Shinnecock's getting its share. These aren't snappers — I've seen teens hooked off the rocks on the last of the outgoing, chopping bunker chunks to pieces before the bass even get a look. If you're throwing metal — a Kastmaster or a Hopkins — off the jetty at dusk into that boiling current edge, you'll know inside three casts whether the blues are stacked up or moved through. Lost a leader to one this week that I'd guess went better than 14 pounds. Bring heavier leader than you think you need.

Inside the bay, the fluke bite has actually turned a corner. It was a slow start to July, but the drift through the flats off Tiana Beach and down toward the Shinnecock Canal mouth has picked up nicely the last ten days. I'm not talking doormats — most fish are running 16 to 19 inches — but there's enough keeper-class fish mixed in that a few boats have had four-fish limits by early afternoon. Standard program: 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet, dragged slow along the sand-to-mud transitions in 12 to 18 feet. Incoming tide has been the better half of the cycle for this — the clean ocean water pushing through the inlet seems to wake the fluke up, where the outgoing gets a little stained and slower.

Ponquogue Bridge is still doing what it does this time of year, which is to say it's producing weakfish for the guys willing to fish it right. That means after dark, that means working the shadow lines the bridge lights throw on the water, and that means fishing the current, not fighting it. I've had my best weakfish on 1/4-ounce bucktails tipped with a strip of squid, cast up-current and let swing back through the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing. Nothing huge — most fish in the 16 to 20-inch class — but there was a 7-plus-pounder weighed in at a Southampton tackle shop this week that tells you the bigger models are still around if you put your time in. Porgies are stacked around those same bridge pilings and the rock piles off Hampton Bays in 15 to 25 feet — clam and squid on a standard porgy rig will keep the rod bent between weakfish bites if you want to fill a cooler.

Nobody's running bass or weakfish through the canal in numbers yet this summer that I've heard of, but with water this warm on both sides, I wouldn't be shocked to hear reports of fish using it as a shortcut into the Peconic on a strong tide change. Worth a look if you're passing through around the lock timing.

Looking ahead, I'd keep working that inlet hole after midnight as long as the ocean stays sloppy — that thermal split between the rough Atlantic and the calmer bay water is exactly what's concentrating bait and bass where they are. If the swell lays down and the ocean cleans up, I'd expect some of that bass and blue activity to spread back out onto the open beach, and the inlet bite could thin out fast. Until then, I'm fishing the dark water and letting the daytime fleet have the sunburn.
